title: Episode 102: The Aroostook Pork and Beans War of 1838: The Bloodless Lumberjack Border War

In 1838 and 1839, the United States and the British Empire mobilized thousands of troops and spent millions of dollars in a tense international border standoff over twelve thousand square miles of prime timber in northern Maine. The total casualties: one man killed by a stray pig and zero battle deaths.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we journey into the dense, snow-choked pine forests of northern Maine and New Brunswick to witness one of the most absurd, colorful, and delightfully bloodless international conflicts in military history: the Aroostook War of eighteen thirty-eight and thirty-nine. Long dubbed the 'Pork and Beans War' after the staple rations that sustained thousands of freezing militiamen, the crisis erupted over twelve thousand square miles of disputed virgin timber along the Aroostook River. When rogue Canadian lumberjacks began illegally poaching prize white pine trees, the State of Maine raised an army, Britain mobilized regulars, and Congress appropriated ten million dollars and fifty thousand troops. In the end, the two great empires settled their differences over a bottle of fine wine and an amiable game of whist. Here is George with the full, hilarious chronicle.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE AMBIGUOUS TREATY OF PARIS
The bizarre roots of the Aroostook War trace back to the Treaty of Paris of seventeen eighty-three, which formally ended the American Revolutionary War. When British and American diplomats drew the northern boundary between the newly independent United States and British North America, they relied on crude, inaccurate maps of the uncharted wilderness. The treaty ambiguously stipulated that the border would run from the source of the St. Croix River along 'the Highlands which divide those rivers that empty themselves into the river St. Lawrence, from those which fall into the Atlantic Ocean.'
Unfortunately, the geography of northern Maine and western New Brunswick contained no single, obvious mountain ridge. Instead, it comprised an undulating labyrinth of dense boreal forests, spruce bogs, and interconnected river basins. For over half a century, both nations made conflicting claims to over twelve thousand square miles of pristine wilderness in the Aroostook River valley—an area larger than the entire states of Massachusetts and Connecticut combined.
For Great Britain, the territory was of supreme strategic military importance. During the winter months, when the St. Lawrence River froze solid, the overland route through the Aroostook Valley was the only direct communication corridor linking the maritime naval base at Halifax, Nova Scotia, with the interior capital of Quebec. For the newly admitted State of Maine—carved out of Massachusetts in eighteen twenty—the valley was a commercial goldmine containing the greatest stands of virgin white pine on the continent. Colonial surveyors had attempted to trace the boundary lines through impenetrable spruce swamps and cedar bogs, leaving behind ambiguous field notes that fueled decades of diplomatic acrimony.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE WHITE PINE FEVER AND THE TIMBER PIRATES
By the eighteen thirties, the Industrial Revolution and a worldwide shipbuilding boom triggered an insatiable demand for massive timber. The majestic eastern white pines of the Aroostook Valley—towering up to two hundred feet tall with trunks five feet in diameter—were prized above all other wood on earth. Known as 'pumpkin pine' for its soft, clear grain, it was ideal for ship masts, wooden hulls, and fine housing construction across Great Britain and the United States.
Because the international boundary remained unadjudicated, the Aroostook territory became a lawless, wild frontier populated by rival timber crews. Every winter, as snow and ice made it possible to drag colossal logs across frozen skid roads, hundreds of Canadian lumberjacks from New Brunswick—known colorfully as 'Provincials'—marched across the border. Operating with the tacit approval of New Brunswick colonial officials, they clear-cut prize timber along the Aroostook and Fish rivers, branding the logs with royal crown marks and floating them down the St. John River to British mills.
To the citizens and politicians of Maine, this was not merely trespassing; it was blatant international piracy and theft of sovereign American resources. Maine newspapers erupted in fury, accusing British poachers of robbing the state of millions of dollars in lumber. In Augusta, newly elected Governor John Fairfield declared that Maine had waited fifty years for the federal government in Washington to resolve the border and would tolerate British plunder no longer. Massive white pine trunks cut from the Aroostook wilderness were floated down the rushing spring rapids, bound into colossal timber rafts that supplied British shipyards constructing Royal Navy men-of-war.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MIDNIGHT KIDNAPPING OF THE LAND AGENT
In January eighteen thirty-nine, Governor Fairfield resolved to take decisive law enforcement action. He appointed Rufus McIntire, a respected former congressman and state land agent, to lead a civilian posse of two hundred armed volunteers into the snow-drifted Aroostook wilderness to arrest illegal Canadian lumber crews and confiscate their equipment.
McIntire's posse marched north through sub-zero blizzards, successfully capturing several Canadian logging camps and impounding thousands of logs. However, on the night of February twelfth, eighteen thirty-nine, while McIntire and his top aides were sleeping at a remote logging cabin near the confluence of the Little Madawaska and Aroostook rivers, a band of forty heavily armed Canadian lumberjacks surrounded the cabin. Kicking down the door, the Canadians dragged McIntire and his companions out into the snow in their nightclothes, bound them with logging ropes, tossed them into open horse sleighs, and hauled them across the border into New Brunswick.
The captured Maine officials were delivered to the jail in Fredericton, New Brunswick, where colonial Lieutenant Governor Sir John Harvey declared them illegal armed invaders. Harvey immediately issued an imperial proclamation declaring Maine's posse an act of unlawful invasion, ordered British militia mobilized, and dispatched regular British troops with artillery to take up positions along the border. Rufus McIntire's civilian posse was authorized to enforce state civil law against foreign timber cartels, but the sudden Canadian midnight raid transformed a local trespass dispute into an international diplomatic crisis.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: MAINE MOBILIZES: THE CALL TO ARMS
When news of the land agent's kidnapping reached Augusta on February fifteenth, eighteen thirty-nine, the State of Maine exploded in patriotic hysteria. In an emergency session, the state legislature voted unanimously to declare a state of war, appropriating eight hundred thousand dollars and ordering ten thousand state militiamen mobilized to march on the frontier.
Across the towns and villages of Maine, fife and drum corps marched through the streets, recruiting volunteers to defend the sovereign honor of the Pine Tree State. Farmers, fishermen, and blacksmiths packed their hunting rifles and marched north into the snowy forests. To sustain the troops through the brutal northern winter, the state quartermasters requisitioned thousands of wooden barrels of salt pork, hardtack crackers, and dried navy beans—prompting soldiers to dub the military campaign the 'Pork and Beans War.'
By early March, over five thousand Maine militiamen were encamped along the Aroostook River, constructing wooden log fortresses including Fort Fairfield and Fort Kent, mounting brass field guns overlooking the frozen waterways. Across the border, Sir John Harvey deployed five hundred British regulars of the Thirty-Fourth and Sixty-Fifth Regiments, supported by hundreds of New Brunswick militia. The two armed camps faced each other across frozen river clearings, muskets loaded, with war between the British Empire and the United States appearing imminent. Volunteers sang rollicking patriotic ballads around northern campfire pits, roasting generous portions of salt pork and navy beans while sharing frontier tales under the sparkling winter stars.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: CONGRESS RALLIES AND GENERAL WINFIELD SCOTT ARRIVES
In Washington, D.C., news of the border crisis sparked national furor. Maine's congressional representatives demanded immediate federal military intervention, declaring that an attack on Maine was an attack on the entire nation. In a rare display of bipartisan unity, Congress passed legislation authorizing President Martin Van Buren to raise fifty thousand federal volunteer troops and appropriated a massive war chest of ten million dollars—an enormous sum in eighteen thirty-nine.
However, President Van Buren and British Prime Minister Lord Melbourne recognized that a full-scale war between the world's greatest naval power and the United States over frozen pine trees would be an absolute economic catastrophe for both nations. Desperate to defuse the powder keg, Van Buren summoned America's preeminent diplomatic troubleshooter: Major General Winfield Scott, the 'Grand Old Man of the Army.'
Standing six feet five inches tall with an imposing military presence and legendary diplomatic charm, General Scott was rushed to Maine with broad executive authority to negotiate a truce. Scott possessed a crucial diplomatic advantage: during the War of 1812, he had been captured by the British and treated with remarkable kindness and chivalry by a young British officer who happened to be none other than Sir John Harvey, the current Governor of New Brunswick. The two opposing commanders were old personal friends. President Van Buren understood that an armed conflict with the British Empire would devastate American international commerce and trigger a catastrophic financial panic in New York and Boston banking houses.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TRUCE OVER WINE AND WHIST
Arriving in Augusta in early March eighteen thirty-nine amidst roaring cheers from patriotic crowds, General Scott immediately began working behind the scenes to cool tempers. He met privately with Governor Fairfield and legislative leaders, urging caution and warning that an accidental musket discharge on the frontier could drag the nation into a bloody, ruinous conflict.
Simultaneously, Scott opened private, affectionate correspondence with his old friend Sir John Harvey across the border. Scott appealed to their shared military honor, proposing that both sides agree to an immediate mutual withdrawal of forces: Maine would withdraw its militia while retaining a small civil posse to prevent timber trespassing, while New Brunswick would withdraw its regular troops and release all American prisoners.
Harvey gladly agreed. Tradition holds that the terms of the armistice were toasted over a fine dinner accompanied by imported port wine and a friendly game of whist. On March twenty-fifth, eighteen thirty-nine, the formal truce was signed. The Maine militiamen packed their knapsacks, finished their remaining rations of pork and beans, and marched triumphantly back to their hometowns to the tune of Yankee Doodle, having defended the border without firing a single shot in anger. General Winfield Scott's chivalrous personal relationship with Sir John Harvey demonstrated the immense power of mutual military respect and gentlemanly integrity in resolving international crises peacefully.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE WEBSTER-ASHBURTON TREATY AND THE PIG CASUALTY
Three years later, in eighteen forty-two, the disputed border was permanently settled in Washington through the historic Webster-Ashburton Treaty, negotiated by United States Secretary of State Daniel Webster and British diplomat Lord Ashburton. Under the compromise agreement, the disputed territory of twelve thousand square miles was partitioned amicably: the United States received seven thousand square miles—giving Maine its modern northern boundary—while Great Britain retained five thousand square miles, securing its vital overland military corridor between Halifax and Quebec.
Remarkably, throughout months of armed mobilization involving over ten thousand heavily armed soldiers facing each other in tense winter conditions, the official casualty count of the Aroostook War was zero battle deaths. Several militiamen tragically died of measles, pneumonia, or hypothermia in winter camps, but the only combat casualty in the entire war was an unfortunate black pig that strayed across a logging trail near Fort Fairfield and was accidentally shot by an over-eager Maine sentinel.
The Aroostook War remains celebrated in Maine and Canadian folklore as a rare, shining triumph of common sense, diplomacy, and personal friendship over the destructive madness of war. Today, along the peaceful, friendly border between Maine and New Brunswick, the original wooden blockhouse of Fort Kent stands preserved as a National Historic Landmark, a whimsical reminder of the great Pork and Beans War and the day two mighty empires chose peace over pine. The successful Webster-Ashburton compromise established the longest undefended international border on earth, inaugurating two centuries of enduring friendship and mutual cooperation between two great nations.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Aroostook War proved that common sense, diplomacy, and gentlemanly friendship could avert a catastrophic war between great empires. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we sail into stormy Penobscot Bay for the surreal disaster of the Royal Tar circus ship.
